fetched_contents.text: Mitochondria Are a Major Source of Paraquat-induced Reactive Oxygen Species Production in the Brain . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2011 May 5. Published in final edited form as: J Biol Chem. 2007 Mar 27;282(19):14186–14193. doi: 10.1074/jbc.M700827200 Abstract Paraquat (PQ2+) is a prototypic toxin known to exert injurious effects through oxidative stress and bears a structural similarity to the Parkinson disease toxicant, 1-methyl-4-pheynlpyridinium. The cellular sources of PQ2+-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, specifically in neuronal tissue, remain to be identified. The goal of this study was to determine the involvement of brain mitochondria in PQ2+-induced ROS production. Highly purified rat brain mitochondria were obtained using a Percoll density gradient method. PQ2+-induced hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) production was measured by fluorometric and polarographic methods. The production of H2O2 was evaluated in the presence of inhibitors and modulators of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. The results presented here suggest that in the rat brain, (a) mitochondria are a principal cellular site of PQ2+-induced H2O2 production, (b) PQ2+-induced H2O2 production requires the presence of respiratory substrates, (c) complex III of the electron transport chain is centrally involved in H2O2 production by PQ2+, and (d) the mechanism by which PQ2+ generates H2O2 depends on the mitochondrial inner transmembrane potential. These observations were further confirmed by measuring PQ2+-induced H2O2 production in primary neuronal cells derived from the midbrain. These findings shed light on the mechanism through which mitochondria may contribute to ROS production by other environmental and endogenous redox cycling agents implicated in Parkinson’s disease. ---------------------------------------- Parkinson disease (PD)2 is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder believed to originate in part via reactive oxygen species (ROS) overproduction, leading to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (1). The disease is characterized pathologically by a progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Both environmental and genetic factors are implicated in specific damage to the nigrostriatal system, contributing to the motor dysfunctions characteristic of PD (2, 3). However, the mechanisms by which such factors cause neurodegeneration remain relatively unknown. Neurotoxins represent the most accepted tools used to produce experimental models of PD both in vivo and in vitro. The most commonly used agents include 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine, 6-hydroxydopamine, rotenone, and paraquat (PQ2+) (4). PQ2+, a member of the widely used bipyridyl herbicides, is a prototypic compound known to exert its toxic effects via oxidative stress. A number of studies have exploited this action of PQ2+to test response and sensitivity to oxidative damage in various models (5–10). The possibility of PQ2+ as a neurotoxin has arisen from evidence that significant damage to the brain is observed in individuals exposed to lethal doses of the herbicide (11, 12). Furthermore, epidemiological studies have suggested an increased risk for developing PD following exposure to the herbicide (13). This has lead to an increased interest in the neurotoxic actions of PQ2+, along with the idea that PQ2+ and other herbicides may act as environmental triggers for PD (14). Therefore, in recent years, PQ2+ has become an increasingly popular model for studying the etiology of PD, alone and also in combination with other environmental toxins (15, 16). Systemic exposure of rodents to PQ2+ has been shown to reproduce many of the pathological features of PD, including selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and presence of intracellular α-synuclein deposits (15, 17–19). Although these studies show that agents such as PQ2+can produce selective neurodegeneration, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying this damage remain unknown. Interestingly, PQ2+ exhibits a remarkable structural similarity to MPP+, the toxic metabolite of 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine. Although both of these compounds are believed to cause toxicity via oxidative stress, PQ2+ exerts its deleterious effects on dopamine neurons in a unique manner compared with MPP+ (20). PQ2+ belongs to a broad class of redox cycling compounds known to produce ROS. The proposed mechanism of redox cycling for PQ2+ involves the enzymatic reduction to form its cationic radical (Fig. 1, reaction 1), which then can reduce molecular oxygen (O2) to superoxide radical ( O2·¯) while also regenerating the parent compound (reaction 2). O2·¯ is subsequently converted to H2O2 either spontaneously (reaction 3) or through the actions of superoxide dismutase (reaction 4). The rate-limiting reaction in this process is the enzymatic reduction of PQ2+ depicted in reaction 1. The identities of enzymes capable of transferring electrons to PQ2+ in this reaction are not completely defined. It is widely accepted that PQ2+-induced generation of ROS arises from a number of cellular sources. Enzymes capable of initiating the redox cycling process of PQ2+ have been identified in microsomal, plasma membrane, and cytosolic components through the actions of NADPH oxidase (21, 22), nitric-oxide synthase (23), and NADPH-cytochrome c reductase (24). However, the role of mitochondria in PQ2+ toxicity is remains unknown. The purpose of this study was to examine the role that mitochondria play in PQ2+-induced ROS production in the brain. This was achieved by measuring rates of H2O2 production using polarographic and fluorometric methods. In particular, mitochondrial components capable of participating in the redox cycling-dependent ROS generation by PQ2+ were examined. It is classified as a viologen, a family of redox-active heterocycles of similar structure.[5] It is one of the most widely used herbicides worldwide. It is quick-acting and non-selective, killing green plant tissue on contact. Paraquat is highly toxic to humans and other animals. The toxicity and lethality depends on the dose and how the herbicide is absorbed by the body. In humans, paraquat damages the mouth, stomach, and intestines if it is ingested orally.[6] Once absorbed in the body, paraquat causes particular damage to the lungs, kidneys, and liver.[6] Paraquat's lethality is attributed to its enhancing production of superoxide anions and human lung cells can accumulate paraquat. Paraquat exposure has been strongly linked to the development of Parkinson's disease.[7] Paraquat may be in the form of salt with chloride or other anions; quantities of the substance are sometimes expressed by cation mass alone (paraquat cation, paraquat ion). The name is derived from the para positions of the quaternary nitrogens. Production and redox reactions Pyridine is coupled by treatment with sodium in ammonia followed by oxidation to give 4,4′-bipyridine. This chemical is then dimethylated with chloromethane to give the final product as the dichloride salt.[8] Use of other methylating agents gives the bispyridinium with alternate counterions. For example, Hugo Weidel's original synthesis used methyl iodide to produce the diiodide.[9] Herbicide use Although first synthesized by Weidel and Russo in 1882,[9] paraquat's herbicidal properties were not recognized until 1955 in the Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) laboratories at Jealott's Hill, Berkshire, England.[10][11] Paraquat was first manufactured and sold by ICI in early 1962 under the trade name Gramoxone, and is today among the most commonly used herbicides. Paraquat is classified as a non-selective contact herbicide. The key characteristics that distinguish it from other agents used in plant protection products are: * It kills a wide range of annual grasses and broad-leaved weeds and the tips of established perennial weeds. * It is very fast-acting. * It is rain-fast within minutes of application. * It is partially inactivated upon contact with soil.[12][13] These properties led to paraquat being used in the development of no-till farming.[14][15][16] The European Union approved the use of paraquat in 2004 but Sweden, supported by Denmark, Austria, and Finland, appealed this decision.[17] In 2007, the court annulled the directive authorizing paraquat as an active plant protection substance stating that the 2004 decision was wrong in finding that there were no indications of neurotoxicity associated with paraquat and that the studies about the link between paraquat and Parkinson's disease should have been considered.[18][19] Thus, paraquat has been banned in the European Union since 2007.[20] China also banned the domestic use of Paraquat in 2017; Thailand followed soon after in 2019 and Brazil, Chile, Malaysia, Peru and Taiwan between 2020 and 2022.[21] India banned it in Odisha in 2023, and temporarily banned it in Kerala in 2011, though the pesticide is still widely used throughout the majority of the country.[22]. fetched_contents.text: Paraquat Induces Cell Death Through Impairing Mitochondrial Membrane Permeability Paraquat Induces Cell Death Through Impairing Mitochondrial Membrane Permeability Huang, CL; Chao, CC; Lee, YC; Lu, MK; Cheng, JJ; Yang, YC; Wang, VC; Chang, WC; Huang, NK Reference Type Journal Article Log in to download HERO ID 2830697 In Press No Year 2015 Title Paraquat Induces Cell Death Through Impairing Mitochondrial Membrane Permeability Authors Huang, CL; Chao, CC; Lee, YC; Lu, MK; Cheng, JJ; Yang, YC; Wang, VC; Chang, WC; Huang, NK Journal Molecular Neurobiology Volume 53 Issue 4 Page Numbers 2169-2188 Abstract Paraquat (PQ) as a Parkinsonian mimetic has been demonstrated to impair dopaminergic (DAergic) neurons and is highly correlated with the etiology of Parkinson's disease (PD) where the death of DAergic neurons has been mainly attributed to impaired mitochondrial functioning. In this study, PQ-induced cytotoxicity focusing on mitochondrial membrane permeability (MMP), which has been implicated to play a part in neurodegeneration, was investigated. Primarily, PQ-induced cytotoxicity and reactive oxygen species (ROS) were inhibited by an inhibitor of NADPH oxidase (NOX), indicating the toxic effect of PQ redox cycling. Further, dibucaine and cyclosporin A which respectively inhibit mitochondrial apoptosis-induced channels (MAC) and mitochondrial permeability transition pores (mPTP) were used and found to prevent PQ-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, such as decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased MMP, mitochondrial ROS, and pro-apoptotic factor release. Knockdown of bax and/or bak blocked PQ-induced mitochondrial clusterization of Bax and/or Bak and cytotoxicity, demonstrating the significance of MAC which is composed of Bax and/or Bak. This clusterization coincided with the release of mitochondrial apoptotic factors before there was an increase in inner MMP, indicating that MAC may precede mPTP formation. Besides, NOX inhibitor but not dibucaine attenuated the earlier PQ-induced cytosolic ROS formation or Bax and/or Bak clusterization indicating PQ redox cycling may account for MAC formation. In this model, we have resolved for the first that PQ cytotoxicity through redox cycling may sequentially result in increased outer (MAC) and inner (mPTP) MMP and suggested MMP could be implicated as a therapeutic target in treating neurodegenerative diseases like PD. Paraquat’s redox cycling mechanism is the central reason it generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) and underlies both its herbicidal action and toxicity. The evidence here is consistent: paraquat is a redox-cycling agent, meaning it accepts electrons from reductants and then donates them back to molecular oxygen, forming radicals and amplifying ROS production [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The mechanism described in the evidence is that paraquat is reduced by enzymes to form a cationic radical, which then reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide anion (O₂·⁻), while regenerating the parent compound [N1-F1]. This cycle is self-sustaining because the reduced paraquat can be reoxidized, allowing it to continue accepting and donating electrons repeatedly [N1-F1].

The ROS produced include superoxide anion (O₂·⁻), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and possibly singlet oxygen, depending on the biological context [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The evidence from mitochondria shows that paraquat can generate H₂O₂ specifically in brain mitochondria, and that this production depends on respiratory substrates and complex III of the electron transport chain [N1-F1]. The same redox cycle is amplified in biological systems because paraquat’s cycle can be initiated by multiple electron donors, including microsomal, plasma membrane, and cytosolic components, and because the cycle can be sustained by the availability of oxygen and reductants [N1-R5][N1-F1]. This amplification is also evident in the evidence that mitochondria contribute to ROS production by other redox-cycling agents, implying that paraquat’s cycle is not a one-off reaction but a recurring, self-reinforcing process [N1-R1][N1-R4].

The redox cycle is self-sustaining because the regenerated paraquat can continue accepting electrons from new reductants and then donating them to oxygen, creating a feedback loop [N1-F1]. In biological systems, this is amplified by the fact that oxygen is abundant, and that many cellular components can act as electron donors, including NADPH oxidase, nitric-oxide synthase, and NADPH-cytochrome c reductase [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that mitochondria are a principal site of paraquat-induced H₂O₂ production, which depends on the mitochondrial inner transmembrane potential and respiratory substrates [N1-F1]. This means that the cycle is not only sustained by the presence of oxygen, but also by the energy state and electron transport capacity of the cell, making it especially potent in metabolically active systems [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Taken together, the redox cycling mechanism explains how paraquat generates ROS: it repeatedly accepts electrons, transfers them to oxygen, and regenerates itself, creating a chain reaction that is self-reinforcing and amplified in oxygen-rich, metabolically active environments [N1-F1][N1-R5]. This is the foundation for both its herbicidal action and its toxicity, as ROS production is a common endpoint in both plant and animal biology.
node_outputs.N9:
In mammals, paraquat toxicity arises primarily because cells become overwhelmed by oxidative stress, which triggers mitochondrial dysfunction, lysosomal damage, and cell death pathways. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that paraquat increases oxidative stress and ROS production, which can induce apoptosis and cell death [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. In the evidence provided, paraquat-induced oxidative stress is linked to mitochondrial membrane permeability, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the release of pro-apoptotic factors, with the redox-cycling pathway being inhibited by NADPH oxidase inhibitors [N3-F3]. This shows that oxidative stress is not just a bystander effect, but a central driver of toxicity.

Mitochondria are a key site of mammalian paraquat toxicity. The evidence states that mitochondria are a principal cellular site of paraquat-induced H₂O₂ production, and that this process requires respiratory substrates and involves complex III of the mitochondrial electron transport chain [N1-F1]. It also notes that mitochondria are a major source of paraquat-induced reactive oxygen species production in the brain [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The mammalian toxicity evidence further reports that paraquat impairs mitochondrial membrane permeability, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial ROS production, while also disrupting mitochondrial permeability transition pores (mPTP) and mitochondrial apoptosis-induced channels (MAC) [N3-F3]. These findings indicate that mitochondria are not just a target of ROS, but an active contributor to toxicity by amplifying oxidative stress and triggering mitochondrial permeability changes that lead to cell death.

Lysosomal involvement is less directly described in the provided evidence, but the broader toxicity context implies that paraquat disrupts intracellular homeostasis beyond mitochondria. The evidence on pulmonary toxicity shows differential responses in Wistar rats and Swiss mice, indicating that toxicity is not uniform across tissues [N4-R1]. In lung tissue, paraquat can increase lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress, and the evidence also notes that paraquat toxicity can affect multiple organs, including the lung, liver, kidney, and brain [N4-R5][N4-R4]. This pattern suggests that lysosomal and other cellular compartments may become stressed as ROS propagate through the cell, but the provided evidence is more focused on mitochondria, apoptosis, and ROS than on lysosomal pathways specifically.

The cell death pathways implicated in mammalian toxicity are primarily apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction. The evidence shows that paraquat-induced cytotoxicity is associated with increased mitochondrial membrane permeability, mitochondrial ROS, and pro-apoptotic factor release, and that inhibition of NADPH oxidase, MAC, or mPTP can prevent mitochondrial dysfunction [N3-F3]. It also reports that paraquat impairs the proteasomal system and that ROS production is a late event in the progression of cell death [N3-R2]. This indicates that toxicity unfolds through multiple steps: oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, release of death signals, and eventual cell death [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3].

Toxicity differs across tissues and species because the evidence shows differential responses in Wistar rats and Swiss mice [N4-R1], and because paraquat toxicity can affect multiple organs, including the lung, liver, kidney, and brain [N4-R5]. The evidence also notes that paraquat toxicity is associated with oxidative stress in the kidney and that rats treated with paraquat show significant increases in lipid peroxidation [N4-R4]. This tissue-specific vulnerability likely reflects differences in redox capacity, oxygen availability, antioxidant defenses, and the relative contribution of mitochondria and other organelles to ROS production and clearance [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence further suggests that species differences may affect the magnitude and pattern of toxicity, as seen in the differential pulmonary responses across strains [N4-R1].

In summary, mammalian toxicity occurs when cells are overwhelmed by oxidative stress generated by paraquat’s redox cycle. Mitochondria are a major site of ROS production and mitochondrial dysfunction, while mitochondrial membrane permeability changes and apoptosis pathways drive cell death [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Toxicity differs across tissues and species because of differential redox handling and organ-specific vulnerability, and the evidence supports the idea that paraquat’s toxicity is a multisystem consequence of ROS overload [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5].

Paraquat’s herbicidal action in plants is rooted in its disruption of photosynthesis and electron transport, particularly through photosystem I. The evidence clearly states that paraquat acts by inhibiting photosynthesis and that it accepts electrons from photosystem I (PSI) [N2-R3][N2-F2]. It also notes that paraquat interferes with PSI by accepting excited electrons and turning them into free radicals, which are highly reactive and disrupt normal electron transport [N2-R1]. This fits with the broader plant-resistance evidence, which reports that paraquat resistance mechanisms involve disrupted transport to the chloroplast and impaired electron transport through PSI [N6-R4]. Thus, the herbicidal mechanism is not simply a general toxicity effect, but a specific interference with the photosynthetic electron transport chain.

The evidence explains how paraquat disrupts electron transport: it accepts electrons from PSI and redirects them into a redox-cycling pathway rather than allowing them to proceed through normal photosynthetic reactions [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This diversion of electrons uncouples the energy of photosynthesis from the biosynthetic machinery, and the evidence states that the energy becomes lethal for the plant cell [N2-R5]. In other words, paraquat does not just block photosynthesis; it causes a metabolic overload by redirecting electrons into a radical-generating cycle that cannot be efficiently dissipated, leading to cell death [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also notes that paraquat has a reciprocal interaction by inhibiting Ca²⁺ influx into plant cells, and that LAT proteins are implicated in resistance mechanisms [N2-R2]. This suggests that plant cells respond to paraquat not only by trying to block uptake and transport but also by altering calcium signaling and transport pathways [N2-R2].

Why plant cells are more vulnerable to ROS than animal cells is not directly spelled out in the provided evidence, but the mechanism strongly implies it. Paraquat’s herbicidal action relies on its ability to accept electrons from PSI and donate them to oxygen, generating radicals and ROS [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. Because plant cells are photosynthetic and operate under light, they may have a higher baseline electron flux and limited antioxidant defenses relative to non-photosynthetic animal cells, making them more susceptible to ROS overload [N2-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that paraquat resistance mechanisms involve uptake, translocation, and sequestration, with some resistance loci disrupting transport to the chloroplast [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This implies that plant cells are not uniformly vulnerable; instead, their vulnerability depends on whether they can absorb, transport, or neutralize paraquat before it reaches its target.

Plant-specific targets and pathways affected by paraquat include photosystem I, electron transport, and chloroplast localization. The evidence explicitly states that paraquat inhibits photosynthesis by accepting electrons from PSI and that resistance mechanisms involve disrupted transport to the chloroplast and impaired electron transport through PSI [N6-R4]. It also notes that LAT proteins are implicated in resistance mechanisms, suggesting that these proteins help regulate uptake or sequestration rather than directly neutralizing the herbicide [N2-R2]. The broader resistance literature indicates that paraquat resistance is studied through uptake, translocation, and sequestration mechanisms, which are central to plant survival after exposure [N6-R2][N6-R5]. This means that the herbicidal action is not just a generic ROS effect, but a specific disruption of the photosynthetic electron transport chain that plants must defend against through specialized resistance pathways [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R4].

Overall, paraquat’s herbicidal action in plants is driven by its ability to accept electrons from photosystem I, disrupt electron transport, and generate ROS through redox cycling [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Plant cells are vulnerable because this disruption can overwhelm the photosynthetic machinery and create a lethal metabolic imbalance [N2-R5]. The plant-specific targets are photosystem I and chloroplast-associated transport pathways, with resistance involving LAT proteins, uptake, translocation, and sequestration mechanisms [N2-R2][N6-R2][N6-R4].

The same redox mechanism can be both herbicidal and toxic because paraquat’s core action—redox cycling and ROS generation—is a general property of biological systems, but the specific consequences depend on the target organism’s biology. In plants, paraquat is herbicidal because it targets photosystem I and disrupts the photosynthetic electron transport chain, whereas in mammals, it is toxic because it overwhelms oxidative stress capacity, especially in mitochondria, and activates cell death pathways [N2-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3][N1-F1]. This dual action is not a coincidence: it is a consequence of the fact that paraquat is a redox-cycling agent that generates radicals and ROS through electron transfer to oxygen, and that different organisms have different redox systems, antioxidant defenses, and organ-specific vulnerabilities [N1-R3][N1-F1][N1-R5].

Plant biology shapes the outcome by making the photosynthetic apparatus a central target. Paraquat accepts electrons from photosystem I, which is a unique feature of plant cells, and this disrupts electron transport in a way that uncouples energy from biosynthesis, creating a lethal metabolic imbalance [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also shows that plant resistance mechanisms involve uptake, translocation, and sequestration, with some resistance loci disrupting transport to the chloroplast and impairing electron transport through PSI [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This means that plant cells are vulnerable because they are photosynthetic, and their survival depends on maintaining a tightly controlled electron flow through photosystem I. In contrast, mammalian cells are vulnerable because their redox systems can be overwhelmed by the same radical-generating cycle [N3-F3][N1-F1].

Mammalian biology shapes the outcome by emphasizing mitochondria, oxidative stress, and cell death pathways. Mitochondria are a major site of paraquat-induced ROS production and mitochondrial dysfunction, and they contribute to ROS generation through complex III of the mitochondrial electron transport chain [N1-F1][N1-R2]. In mammalian toxicity, ROS overload impairs mitochondrial membrane permeability, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial ROS production, while also triggering apoptosis and the release of pro-apoptotic factors [N3-F3]. The evidence further shows that paraquat toxicity is not uniform across tissues and species, with differential responses observed in Wistar rats and Swiss mice and with toxicity affecting multiple organs including the lung, liver, kidney, and brain [N4-R1][N4-R5]. This tissue-specific vulnerability reflects differences in redox capacity, oxygen availability, and organ-specific antioxidant defenses [N4-R4][N4-R5].

This comparative biology has important implications for safety, exposure, and antidote strategies. Because paraquat’s toxicity is driven by ROS overload and mitochondrial dysfunction, exposure control must focus on reducing inhalation, ingestion, and dermal contact, especially in occupational and agricultural settings [N2-F2]. The redox cycle works as follows: paraquat is reduced by enzymes to form a cationic radical, which then reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide anion (O₂·⁻), while regenerating the parent compound [N1-F1]. This cycle is self-sustaining because the reduced paraquat can be reoxidized, allowing it to continue accepting electrons and donating them to oxygen [N1-F1]. The ROS produced include superoxide anion (O₂·⁻), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and possibly singlet oxygen, depending on the biological context [N1-F1][N3-R3]. Mitochondria are a major source of paraquat-induced ROS production, and mitochondrial H₂O₂ production requires respiratory substrates and complex III of the electron transport chain [N1-F1].
